I didn't get time to do a full review earlier or test but I had a look through and I get and agree with the rational for combining the scaling and rotations.

I'm not totally convinced whether the `if` clauses as done here are clearer than before, but I'm sure other reviewers can chip in on that (it's more of a personal taste thing, not crucial either way).

> I'm not totally convinced whether the `if` clauses as done here are clearer than before, but I'm sure other reviewers can chip in on that (it's more of a personal taste thing, not crucial either way).

I tried to reduce repetition of code. One of the reasons for the previous bugs was because global and local were handled in different branching paths, and made maintenance more complicated and error-prone. Now the code is simply retrieving the input matrices differently and applying the output differently, but applying the same syncing operations with the same code.

I also added some clauses to aid with optimization (e.g., simply copying the basis when syncing rotation _and_ scale, which is cheaper than having to treat them individually).

If needed I can add some light commenting. Is there a specific part that you think is less clear?

> Is there a specific part that you think is less clear?

It's not too bad, and I do get the point about duplication, so am having a better look with the code not intermingled (the default github view is kinda hard to follow, so sometimes better to split). Ok on reflection I suppose there is potential for bugs to creep in by duplication here so it's fine as is, just trying to consider the pros and cons.

I think the previous is easier to read for the flow, but your version probably has less bug potential longterm, which is probably more important. :+1: 

It does look fine to me but I've not checked the maths for the order of the operations, but I'm guessing you've tested it thoroughly. I will look later if I get some time, but could do with another reviewer too.

So I've hit a point where I think there needs to be a conversation about the path to take, and it depends on how we want to interpret the user intent when they sync rotation XOR scale when there are negative scales / shearing involved.

Before I go on, I must stress that:
- If no skew or negative scaling is involved, _both_ options work identically and correctly.
- If there is skew or negative scaling, but the entire basis ("rotation + scale") is copied over, _both_ options work identically and correctly.
- However, if skew or negative scaling, _and_ the user wants to sync _only rotation_ or _only scale_, unfortunately we have to acknowledge that this by definition is not possible, and we can only do our best to give them something usable. @aaronfranke's reported issue with negative scaling not working falls under this specific case, but it also was not working before this PR anyway. The following is simply a comparison of two ways we could achieve this.

We know that in Godot, unlike in Unity, there really isn't a separately stored "scale". i.e. there is no reliable, unique scale that can be separated from the basis. The same goes for rotation. The two are inextricably linked through Basis storage. This caveat doesn't really rear its head usually, but sometimes a node's eulers or scale in will change after you reload the scene, because their separation in the inspector is purely a UX layer - a temporary representation.

Unfortunately, the API for `RemoteTransform3D` allows the user to create a separation between "rotation" and "scale" in a way that can/should not allow arbitrary reconciliation like the inspector does. What this leaves us with are two options:

### Option A
Decompose rotation and scale in the same way the inspector does. This is the _current_ behaviour of `RemoteTransform3D`, prior to this PR. The consequences of this are that decomposition and recomposition will happen in a way that can't really be predicted. The GIF below shows what happens when you sync _rotation only_. Note that simply scaling the source transform (i.e. not touching rotation) still causes it to resolve as a rotation change.
![rotation_only](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/01c3d24d-9a0d-4bc4-a730-0c0408d049e8)
In the next GIF, you can see that if you sync _scale only_, the result is also incorrect, which is even more frustrating considering it cannot correctly sync the _only thing_ the user wanted.
![scale_only](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d30ae880-e683-4bdf-8adf-0dca79df6e1e)

### Option B
Decompose into normalized basis + absolute scale (axis lengths). The result is at least understandable and predictable. The GIF below shows what happens when you sync _normalized axes only_. Note that the directionality of every axis is correctly preserved, while the magnitude is ignored.
![rotation_only_B](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/882999b3-26b5-4afd-9af5-3ef6c39d5fd9)
Just for completeness sake, I will also include a GIF of what it looks like syncing _absolute scale_ only, but I must stress that in this new framing, syncing _absolute scale only_ from something that has negative scale is a very strange user intent.
![scale_only_B](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ff547bea-46bf-4ec5-b561-823feff1c850)

My main takeaway from this, and my biggest reason for pushing option B is that its results, albeit oddly specific, are at least _consistent_ and _predictable_, especially if documented. In other words, it at least has _some possibility_ of being useful to _someone_, instead of simply reflecting whatever arbitrary euler-resolving order or axis-resolving order was chosen under the hood. It is also cheaper in comparison, since it only requires calculating/modifying vector lengths.

I've pushed option B for now, at least it solves the issue of nodes rapidly flipping-back-and-forth. Please take a look and toy around with any possibilities you think might come up. This should cover every old use case, correcting some of them, as well as open up some new, niche ones. If we have a good reason for using option A, we could do that too.
